blocks.text: Most human diseases result from microbial infections – invasions of the body by viruses, pathogenic bacteria, fungi, or protists. To defend against infections and against cancers, vertebrates possess a defence system called the immune system. It continually checks the bloodstream for the presence of any foreign cells and molecules. For example, when the immune system detects an infection, it attacks and destroys the invading microbes. That is why, the diseases that weaken the immune system, such as AIDS, are very dangerous.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Our body is defended from infection the same way that a city is defended against foreign invasion. There are walls to make invaders entry difficult, roaming policemen check strangers, security guards challenge anyone wandering and call policeman if a proper ID is not presented. Our body also has different lines of defence.

blocks.alt: A vertical flowchart. Invasive microbe, then FIRST LINE OF DEFENCE, non-specific: skin, digestive tract, respiratory tract. 'If first line of defence is penetrated, the body responds with' SECOND LINE OF DEFENCE, non-specific: killer cells of blood, antimicrobial proteins, inflammation, fever. 'If second line of defence is penetrated, the body responds with' THIRD LINE OF DEFENCE, specific: cell-mediated immunity, antibody-mediated immunity.

blocks.text: The first line of defence against infections consists of skin, the digestive tract, and the respiratory tract.
